title: Proclaim the pilgrimage
hookLine: Ibrahim is told to call people to pilgrimage, and they come on foot and on lean camels from every deep valley (22:27)
last: THE DOG AT THE WELL COUNTS.

lines: AN EMPTY VALLEY, ONE HOUSE OF STONE.
HOW WILL MY VOICE REACH THEM?
cards: A valley with almost nothing in it. Rock, heat, and one small house of stone that an old man and his son have just finished building. No road leads here.
No city. And the old man is told to stand and call all of humanity to come. Commentators report that Ibrahim asked the obvious question: my Lord, how will my voice reach them?
And the answer, as they tell it, was: you call, and the reaching is up to Us. Today, a new surah, Al-Hajj, the Pilgrimage, and that call.

teach.b: Pickthall: "And proclaim unto mankind the Pilgrimage. They will come unto thee on foot and on every lean camel; they will come from every deep ravine".
The verb for proclaim is adhdhin, from the same root as the adhan, the call to prayer, and as udhun, the ear. A call made out loud, meant to be heard. Then look who comes.
On foot, first. Then on every lean camel; the word is damir, thin, worn down from the long road. The verse doesn't picture people arriving rested and polished.

And from every fajj 'amiq, every deep mountain pass, the kind of narrow gap between hills a road squeezes through. The camels have changed. Pilgrims now come by plane and bus, from Jakarta and Lagos and Detroit.
They come from every valley, still.

On the way, pilgrims repeat the talbiya over and over: labbayk allahumma labbayk. Here I am, O God, here I am. Some commentators connect that line with this verse: an answer to a call made in an empty valley.
Not everyone can go. The Qur'an makes Hajj a duty only for those able to make the journey. But the picture belongs to everyone: thin camels, tired feet, and a voice that somehow carried.

how: Muslims who are physically and financially able make the Hajj to Mecca at least once in their lives, in the month of Dhul-Hijjah, repeating the talbiya, 'labbayk allahumma labbayk', as they travel.

o: the walk around the Ka'ba seven times over
the call to prayer from a mosque's minaret
the pilgrims' call: here I am, O God, here I am

games.q: inside the call — tap the pairs.
p: proclaim, call out so ears hear
lean, worn down from the road

s: the verse pictures pilgrims arriving rested and well supplied
on foot, and on lean camels, worn thin by the road.
adhdhin shares a root with the adhan, the call to prayer
and with udhun, the ear: a call made to be heard.
the Qur'an makes Hajj a duty for every Muslim, able or not
it is a duty for those able to make the journey.

games.q: you're Ibrahim, standing in an empty valley. you've been told to call all of humanity to come. what do you do?
o: wait until there's a road and a town.
ask how your voice could reach them, then call anyway.
send messengers to the nearest tribes instead.
games.why: commentators report he asked how his voice would reach, and was told: you call, the reaching is up to Us. so he called.

practice: Picture one pilgrim coming down a mountain road on foot, then another from a desert, then a bus from a city you've never visited, a plane full of grandmothers, a young man who saved for ten years.
Let the roads fill until you can't count them. If you pray, you can pray for the ones on the road right now.

wordCard.voice: Talbiya. The pilgrims' repeated call, here I am, O God, here I am, answering Ibrahim's call from an empty valley. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: proclaim, call out; from the same root as adhan, the call to prayer.

carryVoice: Your line: they come from every valley. Far roads, one answer: here I am. Day four hundred eighty-five.
